front_blocks.md: Define **covalent bond**.

back_blocks.md: A **covalent bond** is the electrostatic attraction between the nuclei of two non-metal atoms and their shared pair of electrons in the outer shell.

cards.front_md: Define **covalent bond**.
cards.back_md: A **covalent bond** is the electrostatic attraction between the nuclei of two non-metal atoms and their shared pair of electrons in the outer shell.

front_blocks.md: How many electrons are shared in a single, double and triple covalent bond?

back_blocks.md: A **single** bond shares **2** electrons (1 pair), a **double** bond shares **4** electrons (2 pairs), and a **triple** bond shares **6** electrons (3 pairs).

cards.front_md: How many electrons are shared in a single, double and triple covalent bond?

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
In covalent bonding, electrons are transferred from one atom to the other.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
In covalent bonding, electrons are **shared** between the two atoms. Electron transfer occurs in ionic bonding, not covalent bonding.

back_blocks.md: In N<sub>2</sub>, the two nitrogen atoms share **three** pairs of electrons, forming a **triple** covalent bond.

front_blocks.md: What is meant by 'expanding the octet rule', and give one example?

back_blocks.md: Expanding the octet means a central atom accommodates **more than 8 electrons** in its outer shell. For example, sulfur in SF<sub>6</sub> has a share of **12 electrons**, forming six single S-F bonds.

Covalent bonding can occur between a metal and a non-metal.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
Covalent bonding occurs between **two non-metals**. Bonding between a metal and a non-metal typically involves ionic bonding.

front_blocks.md: Why does PCl<sub>5</sub> have an expanded octet, and how many electrons does phosphorus share in this molecule?

back_blocks.md: Phosphorus uses available d orbitals to accommodate more than 8 electrons. In PCl<sub>5</sub>, phosphorus forms **5 single bonds** and has a share of **10 electrons**, exceeding the normal octet.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Sharing electrons in a covalent bond allows each atom to achieve a noble gas electron configuration.

back_blocks.md: **True.**
Sharing electrons gives each atom a full outer shell similar to a noble gas configuration, increasing the stability of both atoms.

front_blocks.md: Define **coordinate bond**.

back_blocks.md: A **coordinate bond** (dative covalent bond) is a covalent bond in which both electrons in the shared pair are donated by the same atom, which must possess a lone pair.

cards.front_md: Define **coordinate bond**.

front_blocks.md: How is the ammonium ion (NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>) formed, and which atom provides both electrons in the coordinate bond?

back_blocks.md: The **nitrogen** atom in ammonia donates its lone pair of electrons to the electron-deficient H<sup>+</sup> ion, forming a coordinate bond. Both electrons in this bond come from the nitrogen atom, producing NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>.

front_blocks.md: Define **electron-deficient atom**.

back_blocks.md: An **electron-deficient atom** is an atom that has an unfilled outer orbital and can therefore accept a lone pair of electrons to form a coordinate bond.

front_blocks.md: Why does AlCl<sub>3</sub> form a dimer (Al<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>6</sub>) at lower temperatures?

back_blocks.md: AlCl<sub>3</sub> is **electron-deficient** (aluminium has an incomplete outer shell). At lower temperatures, lone pairs on chlorine atoms of one AlCl<sub>3</sub> molecule form **two coordinate bonds** with aluminium atoms of a second AlCl<sub>3</sub> molecule, giving the more stable dimer Al<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>6</sub>.

Once formed, a coordinate bond is identical in strength and properties to an ordinary covalent bond.

After formation, a coordinate bond is indistinguishable from an ordinary covalent bond. The distinction lies only in the origin of the electrons, not in the bond itself.

back_blocks.md: The atom must possess a **lone pair** of electrons (a non-bonding pair) in its outer shell that it can donate to an electron-deficient atom.

front_blocks.md: Define **hybridisation**.

back_blocks.md: **Hybridisation** is the mixing of atomic orbitals within the same shell to form new hybrid orbitals of equal energy, used to explain the bonding and geometry of covalent molecules.

front_blocks.md: What orbitals combine to form sp<sup>3</sup> hybrid orbitals, and what geometry do they produce?

back_blocks.md: One **s orbital** and three **p orbitals** mix to form four sp<sup>3</sup> hybrid orbitals. These arrange with **tetrahedral geometry**, giving bond angles of **109.5°** (e.g. in methane, CH<sub>4</sub>).

front_blocks.md: Define **pi (π) bond**.

back_blocks.md: A **pi (π) bond** is formed by the sideways overlap of adjacent p orbitals, with electron density distributed above and below the plane of the sigma bond.

front_blocks.md: How many sigma bonds and pi bonds are in a carbon-carbon triple bond (as in ethyne)?

back_blocks.md: A triple bond contains **one sigma (σ) bond** and **two pi (π) bonds**. The sigma bond arises from end-on overlap and the two pi bonds from sideways overlap of two pairs of p orbitals at right angles to each other.

front_blocks.md: What hybridisation does nitrogen adopt in ammonia, and how does the lone pair affect the bond angle compared to methane?

back_blocks.md: Nitrogen in NH<sub>3</sub> is **sp**<sup>**3**</sup> hybridised. The lone pair occupies one sp<sup>3</sup> orbital and repels the bonding pairs more strongly than bonding pairs repel each other, reducing the bond angle to **107°** (compared to 109.5° in CH<sub>4</sub>).

front_blocks.md: Define **bond energy**.

back_blocks.md: **Bond energy** is the energy required to break one mole of a particular covalent bond in the gaseous state, measured in kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>. A larger bond energy indicates a stronger bond.

back_blocks.md: Going from single to triple bond: bond length **decreases** (single <sub>147 pm, double </sub>134 pm, triple <sub>120 pm) and bond energy </sub>**<sub>increases</sub>**<sub> (single </sub>347 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>, double <sub>614 kJ mol</sub><sup><sub>-1</sub></sup><sub>, triple </sub>839 kJ mol<sup>-1</sup>). Triple bonds are the shortest and strongest.

A longer bond length corresponds to a stronger covalent bond.

back_blocks.md: **False.**
A longer bond length means the nuclei are further apart and the attractive forces are weaker, so the bond is **weaker**. Shorter bonds are stronger.

front_blocks.md: Why does bond energy decrease in the order HCl > HBr > HI?

back_blocks.md: Going down the halogen group, the atoms become larger. The bonding electrons are further from the nucleus and experience greater shielding, so the **attractive force between bonding electrons and nucleus decreases**, making the bond easier to break.
